title: Five ways El Niño is affecting weather around the world
description:
El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.

Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.

The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.

BBC reporter William Lee Adams speaks with BBC weather presenter and meteorologist Sarah Keith-Lucas. She explains five ways its impact is already being felt around the world. Plus we hear from people experiencing the impact of extreme weather events in Singapore, India and Japan.

summaryEn: This episode of the BBC podcast What in the World examines five ways the strengthening El Niño phenomenon is affecting global weather patterns. BBC weather presenter and meteorologist Sarah Keith-Lucas explains how elevated Pacific Ocean temperatures are driving severe weather events across the globe. In Southeast Asia, drier and hotter weather has triggered Indonesia's worst wildfire season since 2015, spreading toxic haze to Singapore and causing widespread respiratory illness. In the Eastern Pacific, warmer waters are supercharging hurricane formation, whereas the Atlantic has seen an unusually quiet hurricane season due to strong winds tearing storms apart. In India, a weak monsoon season has brought reduced rainfall, threatening farming and food prices. Meanwhile, East Asia—including Japan, Taiwan, and eastern China—faces record-breaking rainfall and powerful typhoons like Super Typhoon Chan-hom. The World Meteorological Organization warns that these extreme weather impacts will persist into early 2024.
